title: Portuguese Africa
capsule: Portuguese Africa designates the collective coastal and island holdings Portugal accumulated in sub-Saharan Africa from its first permanent post at Arguin (1445) through the early sixteenth century, when a network of fortified feitorias anchored trade in gold, ivory, and enslaved persons along the Atlantic coast. Key installations included São Jorge da Mina on the Gold Coast (1481), the island colony of São Tomé (settled from c. 1485), and a network of posts along the Kongo and Angola coasts. Administration remained rudimentary — Portugal governed through royal trading monopolies and local intermediaries rather than territorial occupation — and the Estado da India framework applied overseas holdings collectively. The period 1580–1640 marked the Iberian Union, when Portugal and its overseas territories passed under Philip II of Spain, interrupting the purely Portuguese character of these holdings.
attestation: Boundaries from Seshat Cliopatria (Bennett et al., Scientific Data 2025; CC BY 4.0), digitized from standard historical atlases at ~0.07° resolution. The coastal trading-post network is well documented, but this entity's boundaries as a mapped polity are highly uncertain — Portugal exercised influence over scattered coastal points rather than contiguous territory, making any polygon representation a significant simplification.
